scams.name: Nanjing Road Tea House / Bar Scam
scams.description:
You are walking along Nanjing Road's pedestrian strip when two young people approach in fluent English. They say they are visiting from Xi'an and invite you to experience a traditional tea ceremony nearby. The conversation is warm and natural — they know the landmarks, seem genuinely curious about your trip, and the suggestion feels like a lucky local encounter.

Within ten minutes you are in a small tea house on a side street. The tea tastes fine. Then the bill arrives: ¥3,000 to ¥10,000. The staff are no longer welcoming. A bouncer stands near the door. You are expected to pay in full before you leave. A venue at 510 Tianjin Road has been specifically named in multiple traveler reports as running this operation continuously for years.

Any stranger near Nanjing Road, People's Square, or the Bund who invites you to a 'tea ceremony' or 'cultural experience' within minutes of meeting is running this scam — walk past with 'bu yao, xie xie' and do not engage further. For genuine Shanghai tea, the Huxinting Teahouse at Yu Garden has operated since 1855 with posted prices of ¥150–¥300 per person. If you do get trapped, pay by credit card rather than cash for a chargeback route, and report the venue to 12315 — China's consumer-protection English hotline.
scams.avoidance: Walk past any stranger approaching near Nanjing Road with 'bu yao xie xie' Never follow a stranger to a 'nearby' tea house — the venue is always the scam Avoid 510 Tianjin Road (SMOOTH dining bar) and any similar side-street 'tea' venue For genuine tea, go to Shanghai Propaganda Poster Art Centre cafe or hotel-concierge-recommended venues If trapped, photograph the bill, pay with credit card (for chargeback leverage), then report to 12315 and your card company
scams.location: Nanjing Road East and West pedestrian shopping area, side streets off People's Square, Tianjin Road, Bund approach
scams.tldr: Pairs of friendly locals approach tourists on Nanjing Road and near People's Square in fluent English with an invitation to a 'traditional tea ceremony' — then escort victims to locked side-street teahouses where bills of ¥3,000–¥10,000 arrive and exits are blocked by bouncers until payment is made.

scams.name: Pudong (PVG) Airport Black Taxi & Meter Rigging
scams.description:
You clear customs at Pudong Airport and follow the ground transportation signs. Before you reach the official taxi queue, men in casual dress step forward: 'Taxi to Shanghai city? Four hundred yuan, very cheap.' The legitimate metered fare from PVG to central Shanghai is ¥180–¥220 for the 45-kilometer, 50-minute trip.

The driver takes your luggage and leads you to a car in an unofficial pickup zone. There is no meter running, or the meter advances noticeably faster than the standard rate. At the destination, a surprise luggage surcharge appears before the driver will open the boot. If you take the Maglev to Longyang Road and then try to grab a taxi, the overcharging is even more concentrated there than at the airport itself.

Install DiDi before you land — it has an English interface, regulated fares, and a digital receipt — or take Shanghai Metro Line 2 from Pudong Airport station to People's Square for ¥7 in 90 minutes, which is completely scam-proof. If you do take a licensed taxi, say 'da biao' (打表 — run the meter) before boarding, screenshot a DiDi fare estimate as a benchmark, and photograph the taxi license number from the rear windscreen. If you take the Maglev, connect to Metro Line 2 or 7 at Longyang Road rather than picking up a taxi there.
scams.avoidance: Take Shanghai Metro Line 2 from PVG station: ¥7, 90 min, scam-proof Install DiDi before arrival; English interface, regulated fares, digital receipt If taking licensed taxi, say 'da biao' (打表) before boarding; screenshot DiDi fare as reference Photograph the taxi license number from the rear windscreen on entering If you take the Maglev, transfer to Metro Line 2/7 at Longyang Road, not a taxi
scams.location: Pudong International Airport (PVG) arrivals hall, official taxi queue, Longyang Road Maglev terminus, Hongqiao Airport (SHA) secondary
scams.tldr: Unlicensed taxi touts intercept tourists at Pudong Airport before they reach the official queue, quoting flat fares of ¥400–¥600 to central Shanghai — roughly double the legitimate metered rate of ¥180–¥220 — while even licensed cabs at the Longyang Road Maglev terminus have documented cases of tampered meters running at inflated rates.

scams.name: Bund & People's Square Wine / Champagne Bar Overcharge
scams.description:
You are walking along the Bund enjoying the Pudong skyline when an attractive, English-speaking person strikes up conversation. They mention a rooftop bar with a genuine river view that most tourists never find. The bar is real, the view is real, and the ambiance is exactly as described — everything about the encounter feels like a lucky local tip.

Once seated, your companion orders 'just one drink.' A bottle of champagne arrives instead. No prices were posted at the entrance or on the table. The bill that follows is ¥6,000 to ¥20,000. When you object, the mood changes quickly — staff cluster near the exit and your companion has vanished. The bar's own posted menu, if it exists at all, often lists the same inflated prices, meaning you technically agreed to them.

Never follow a stranger from the Bund or Nanjing Road to a bar they recommend — only enter venues you chose yourself with a posted English menu and card payment confirmed before you sit down. Legitimate Bund-view bars with verified pricing include M on the Bund, Bar Rouge, the Waldorf Astoria's Long Bar, and the Peace Hotel's Jazz Bar. If you are trapped, pay by credit card for a chargeback route, photograph the bill and menu, and file a report with your card issuer and with 12315.
scams.avoidance: Choose Bund-view bars yourself: M on the Bund, Bar Rouge, Hakkasan, Waldorf Long Bar, Peace Hotel Jazz Bar (all posted pricing, booking required) Walk past any stranger offering a 'local bar' invitation on the Bund Always verify a bar has posted English menu and card payment BEFORE ordering Pay with credit card for chargeback leverage; cash and Alipay are much harder to dispute If trapped, photograph the bill and inflated prices; dispute via card and report to 12315
scams.location: Bars near the Bund, Nanjing Road East/West side streets, People's Square north side, Xintiandi tourist-facing venues
scams.tldr: A friendly English-speaking local approaches tourists on the Bund and leads them to an unmarked upper-floor bar under the pretext of a 'perfect sunset view,' then orders a bottle of champagne that triggers a bill of ¥6,000–¥20,000 — with staff blocking the exit until it is paid in full.

scams.name: Shanghai Tea Ceremony Ambush at Yuyuan & The Bund
scams.description:
You are exploring the narrow lanes of Yu Garden's bazaar when someone approaches: 'Excuse me, we are students — could you help us practice English?' or 'Could you take a photo of us?' The interaction seems harmless and the person appears genuinely curious. Conversation flows naturally about your travel plans before a 'traditional tea ceremony nearby' is suggested a few minutes in.

The venue is a few blocks off the main bazaar walkway — up a staircase, or through an unmarked door. Tea is served and the atmosphere is pleasant. Then the bill arrives: ¥800 to ¥2,500 per person — ten to twenty times the ¥150–¥300 that the legitimate Huxinting Teahouse inside Yu Garden charges. Police historically take the venue's side on the grounds that you agreed to attend voluntarily.

Walk past anyone at Yu Garden, the Bund, or People's Square who approaches with a request to 'practice English' or 'help with a photo' — the tea ceremony invitation always follows within minutes. For authentic tea at Yu Garden, go directly to the Huxinting Teahouse — the pavilion in the middle of the pond, in operation since 1855 — with prices of ¥150–¥300 per person and a clearly posted menu. If you are overcharged, pay by credit card and file a chargeback alongside a report to 12315.
scams.avoidance: Walk past any stranger at Yu Garden, Bund, or People's Square offering 'English practice' or 'photo help' For genuine tea at Yu Garden, visit Huxinting Teahouse (the pavilion in the middle of the pond, 1855) Published tea prices at Huxinting: ¥150–¥300 per person with clear menu Never follow a stranger to a 'nearby' tea house, even if they seem friendly Pay with credit card for chargeback leverage; report via 12315 and your card issuer
scams.location: Yu Garden (Yuyuan) bazaar area, the Bund promenade, People's Square south side, pedestrian shopping zones
scams.tldr: A softer variant of the Nanjing Road teahouse scam runs at Yu Garden's bazaar and along the Bund — strangers asking to 'practice English' or requesting help with a photo pivot to a 'nearby tea ceremony' within minutes, with bills of ¥800–¥2,500 arriving at side-street venues charging ten to twenty times the legitimate price.

scams.name: Shanghai Disneyland 'Fast Pass' & Fake Ticket Scams
scams.description:
You are planning a day at Shanghai Disneyland and search for Premier Access passes to skip the longest queues. A reseller or hotel lobby booth offers fast-track entry at ¥800 per person. The official rate is ¥300–¥600 depending on demand, sold only through the Shanghai Disneyland app or entrance kiosks. A tout near the Disney Resort Metro station offers even cheaper QR-code tickets that look authentic in a screenshot.

At the gate, the scanner rejects your QR code. The third-party seller is unreachable — typically a WeChat contact with no physical address. If you bought from a hotel lobby tout, the hotel cannot help either. The Premier Access markup is subtler: the pass works, but you paid 1.5 to 2 times the legitimate price for a product available directly from Disney. In both cases the money is gone with no recovery path.

Book all Shanghai Disneyland tickets — entry, Premier Access, and dining — directly through the official Shanghai Disneyland app or at shanghaidisneyresort.com, and pay with a credit card for fraud protection. Disney Premier Access costs ¥300–¥600 through official channels; anything higher from a third party is a markup or counterfeit. Metro Line 11 to Disney Resort station costs ¥5–¥7 from central Shanghai in 40 minutes — avoid any package tour that bundles transportation and tickets.
scams.avoidance: Book directly via Shanghai Disneyland official app or shanghaidisneyresort.com Disney Premier Access is ¥300–¥600; anything higher is a markup or scam Shanghai Metro Line 11 to Disney Resort station: ¥5–¥7, 40 min, scam-proof Pay with credit card for fraud protection; avoid cash/Alipay for chargeback reasons For hotel stays, book only Disney Resort Hotel or Toy Story Hotel via Disney's own site
scams.location: Shanghai Disneyland main entrance (Pudong), Disney Resort Metro station, third-party resale sites, hotel-concierge packages
scams.tldr: Touts near the Disney Resort Metro station and on third-party resale sites sell fake Shanghai Disneyland Premier Access passes at ¥700–¥800 per person — well above the official ¥300–¥600 rate — or outright counterfeit QR-code tickets that are rejected at the gate with no refund recourse since the seller is untraceable.

scams.name: AP Xinyang Fake Market Bait-and-Switch
scams.description:
AP Xinyang and Han City are open markets where vendors sell replica brand goods in a legal-grey environment well known on Shanghai's tourist circuit. You examine a replica watch that looks and feels solid, negotiate the price from ¥500 down to ¥200, and feel good about the deal. The vendor smiles and says they will wrap it for you in the back.

The item returned from the back is a lower grade than what you examined — a thinner case, different movement, noticeably lighter. The switch happened in the thirty seconds the vendor spent out of your line of sight. In the jewelry variant, a handheld 'diamond tester' is used to 'prove' a stone in a replica Rolex is real — the device is rigged or deliberately misread. Beyond the switch itself, bringing counterfeit goods home is illegal in the US, UK, and EU, where customs can confiscate them on arrival.

Hold the exact item you examined from inspection through payment — never let a vendor take it to 'wrap in the back' or 'check the price' in a separate area. Start any negotiation at 10–15% of the first-quoted price and walk away if refused. For genuine shopping with returns and honest pricing, Global Harbor, Xintiandi, and IFC Mall are all within central Shanghai and require no negotiation.
scams.avoidance: Start negotiations at 10–15% of first-quoted price; walk away if vendor refuses Hold the specific item yourself from inspection through payment; refuse 'wrapping in back' Understand home-country customs prohibit commercial counterfeits; personal-use amounts vary but risks are real Consider alternatives: Global Harbor, Xintiandi, IFC Mall for genuine shopping with returns If shopping anyway, budget only what you can afford to lose entirely
scams.location: AP Xinyang Fashion Market (Science & Technology Museum metro), Han City Fashion & Accessories Plaza, various 'underground fake' markets
scams.tldr: Vendors at AP Xinyang Fashion Market near Science & Technology Museum metro and Han City in Jing'an show tourists a high-quality replica item during negotiation, then switch it for a lower-grade product at the moment of wrapping — or use rigged 'diamond testers' to convince buyers that counterfeit jewelry is genuine, with no returns possible after leaving the stall.

scams.name: Pudong Airport SIM Card Tout Markup
scams.description:
You clear customs at Pudong and immediately need data — your home carrier's international roaming is expensive and you want a local SIM. A booth in the arrivals corridor or a man in casual dress approaches: 'Tourist SIM card, 30GB, 30 days, ¥300.' The price sounds reasonable after a long flight. The identical plan from China Mobile or China Unicom at their official airport counters costs ¥100–¥150.

The tout's SIM activates and appears to work. Two days later, connectivity drops. The seller has no counter number, the receipt is illegible, and the WeChat contact goes silent. Even when the SIM works for the full trip, you paid two to three times the standard rate for a product available thirty meters away at an official carrier booth. A common variant sells a ¥300 'tourist plan' that actually contains only 5GB buried in a confusing tariff structure.

Buy your China SIM directly from the China Unicom or China Mobile counter in the Pudong Terminal 2 arrivals hall — both sell 30-day 30GB tourist plans for ¥100–¥150 with an official fapiao receipt. The cleanest option for most travelers is an eSIM from Airalo or Holafly purchased before departure — it activates before you land and eliminates any airport counter visit. Ignore all booths and individuals in the arrivals hall that are not clearly branded with the carrier's official logo.
scams.avoidance: Buy an eSIM before flying: Airalo, Holafly, or Nomad sells China 5GB 30-day at US$15–US$30 At PVG, use ONLY the official China Unicom or China Mobile counter — ¥100–¥150 for 30 days/30GB Ignore any SIM booth not clearly carrier-branded For short trips (<10 days), home-carrier roaming is often competitive Keep a receipt (fapiao) from whichever carrier you choose for any warranty or support needs
scams.location: Pudong Airport arrivals hall, along airport transit paths, hotel check-in desks offering 'tourist SIM' packages
scams.tldr: Unofficial booths and freelance touts in Pudong Airport's arrivals hall sell 'tourist SIM' packages for ¥300 — two to three times the ¥100–¥150 price of the identical plan at the official China Mobile or China Unicom counters nearby — and sometimes sell SIMs that stop working within seven days.
